main_competence_name: Demonstrate mastery of the structure of the Earth
specific_competence_name: Demonstrate an Advanced understanding of concepts and theories explaining the structure of the Earth and the interactions of earth systems
learning_activity_name: Describe the theories (continental drift, Isostacy and plate tectonics) that explain the gross structure of the earth’s surface (continents, oceans, seas, ocean ridges, ocean trenches, Islands etc.)
sla_name: Theories of the Structure of the Earth's Surface
sla_assessment_criteria: The theories that explain the gross structure of the earth’s surface are well described.
sla_teaching_aids: Online resources on theories that explain the gloss structure of the Earth’s surface|Globe|World map
sla_references: TET(2023), GEOGRAPHY SYLLABUS FOR ADVANCED SECONDARY EDUCATION FORM V-VI, TET, DAR ES SALAAM
sla_notes_intro: The earth's surface is made of continents and oceans whose positions are explained by scientific theories. The main theories are continental drift, isostasy and plate tectonics.
sla_notes_details: Continental drift (Alfred Wegener, 1912) proposed that a single supercontinent, Pangaea, broke apart and continents drifted, supported by the fit of coastlines, fossil and rock similarities and climatic evidence. Isostasy explains vertical balance: lighter crust floats on denser mantle, so mountains have deep roots and rise when material is removed. Plate tectonics states that the lithosphere is divided into plates moving over the asthenosphere, driven by convection currents, ridge push and slab pull. Plate boundaries are divergent (ocean ridges, rift valleys), convergent (trenches, fold mountains, island arcs) and transform (faults). These processes account for continents, oceans, seas, ocean ridges and trenches and islands.
sla_notes_illustrations: The East African Rift Valley is a divergent boundary where the African plate is splitting into Nubian and Somali plates, producing Lakes Tanganyika and Malawi and volcanoes such as Ol Doinyo Lengai.
sla_notes_daily_life: Earthquakes felt in Kagera or volcanic activity near Arusha are everyday evidence of plate movements.
sla_exercise: Who proposed the theory of continental drift?::Alfred Wegener.||Name the three types of plate boundaries.::Divergent, convergent and transform.||Give one piece of evidence for continental drift.::The fit of the coasts of Africa and South America (or matching fossils).

learning_activity_name: Describe the interactions among the major earth systems (atmosphere, biosphere, hydrosphere, geosphere)
sla_name: Interactions Among the Major Earth Systems
sla_assessment_criteria: The interactions among the major earth systems are well described.
sla_teaching_aids: Online resources on major earth systems|Diagrams on the interaction among the major earth systems
sla_references: TET(2023), GEOGRAPHY SYLLABUS FOR ADVANCED SECONDARY EDUCATION FORM V-VI, TET, DAR ES SALAAM
sla_notes_intro: The earth is made of four connected systems: atmosphere, hydrosphere, geosphere and biosphere. They exchange matter and energy continuously.
sla_notes_details: The atmosphere is the layer of gases, the hydrosphere is all water, the geosphere is rocks and soil and the biosphere is all living things. They interact through cycles: the water cycle links atmosphere and hydrosphere, the carbon cycle links all four (photosynthesis, respiration, burning), and weathering links atmosphere, water and rocks to form soil that supports plants. Human activities such as deforestation, mining, pollution and burning of fossil fuels alter these interactions, causing climate change, soil erosion and loss of biodiversity. Sustainable use maintains balance.
sla_notes_illustrations: Rain (atmosphere) falls on mountain slopes, weathers rock (geosphere), feeds rivers (hydrosphere) and supports forests (biosphere); deforestation upsets this chain by increasing runoff and floods.
sla_notes_daily_life: The interactions explain why cutting trees near a river dries the river and reduces rain, affecting farmers.
sla_exercise: Name the four major earth systems.::Atmosphere, hydrosphere, geosphere and biosphere.||Which cycle connects atmosphere and hydrosphere?::The water (hydrological) cycle.||Give one human activity that disturbs earth systems.::Deforestation.

main_competence_name: Demonstrate mastery of the structure of the Earth
specific_competence_name: Demonstrate an understanding of the forces responsible for formation of the major relief features of the Earth
learning_activity_name: Describe the internal forces responsible for the formation of the Earth’s major relief features (volcanoes, block mountains, fold mountains, faults, rift valleys, depressions/basin) and earthquakes
sla_name: Internal Forces and Major Relief Features
sla_assessment_criteria: The internal forces responsible for the formation of the Earth’s major relief features are well described.
sla_teaching_aids: Diagrams|Maps|Atlas of the physical features|Models of the features result from internal forces|ICT device with contents on internal forces
sla_references: TET(2023), GEOGRAPHY SYLLABUS FOR ADVANCED SECONDARY EDUCATION FORM V-VI, TET, DAR ES SALAAM
sla_notes_intro: Internal (endogenic) forces originate inside the earth and build relief features. They include folding, faulting, volcanism and earthquakes.
sla_notes_details: Folding, caused by compressional forces, produces fold mountains such as the Alps and Himalayas. Faulting, caused by tension or compression, produces block mountains (horsts), rift valleys (grabens), and depressions or basins. Volcanic activity produces volcanoes such as Kilimanjaro and Meru, calderas and lava plateaus. Earthquakes are sudden vibrations from movement along faults, with a focus and epicentre and measured by the Richter scale and seismographs. Effects are landform creation, loss of life, damage and tsunamis, and hazards are reduced by early warning, building codes and community mapping.
sla_notes_illustrations: The Usambara block mountains and Lake Tanganyika rift valley show faulting: land between two parallel faults dropped to form a graben in the case of the lake.
sla_notes_daily_life: Communities near volcanoes or fault zones learn evacuation routes and safe building methods to reduce hazard impacts.
sla_exercise: What forces produce fold mountains?::Compressional forces.||Define a rift valley.::A long depression formed when land between parallel faults subsides.||Which instrument records earthquakes?::A seismograph.

sla_notes_intro: External (exogenic) forces act on the surface and shape it by weathering, erosion, transportation and deposition. The main agents are waves, gravity, wind and running water.
sla_notes_details: Running water creates valleys, gullies, waterfalls, meanders, flood plains and deltas. Wind creates yardangs, zeugens, deflation hollows, sand dunes and loess. Waves create cliffs, wave-cut platforms, caves, arches, stacks, beaches and spits. Gravity causes mass movements such as landslides, soil creep and rock falls. Rate of change depends on climate, rock type, slope and vegetation. The resulting landforms have importance for agriculture, tourism, settlement and hydropower but also produce hazards.
sla_notes_illustrations: The Rufiji delta was created when the river slowed on entering the Indian Ocean and deposited sediment, forming fertile land for rice and mangroves.
sla_notes_daily_life: Gullies in farmland show soil erosion and lead people to practise terracing and afforestation.
sla_exercise: Name two landforms made by running water.::Valleys and deltas (or flood plains, gullies).||Which landform is formed by wind erosion in deserts?::A yardang or zeugen.||What is mass wasting?::Downslope movement of soil and rock due to gravity.

sla_teaching_aids: Diagrams of the surveying tools|Activities ranging poles|Pegs|Chains|Tapes|Cross staff|Arrow|Alidade|Spirit level|Notebook|Compass|Abney level|Plane table|Tripod stands|Pins|Drawing accessories|U folk|Plumb bob|Telescopic alidade|GPS|GIS|ICT device with contents on surveying activities

sla_notes_intro: Surveying measures and records the positions and heights of features on the ground to prepare maps. Advanced methods include plane table, prismatic compass and levelling.
sla_notes_details: Plane tabling uses a drawing board on a tripod, alidade and ranging poles to plot features directly in the field by methods of radiation, intersection, traversing and resection. The prismatic compass measures bearings and is used in traversing, with corrections for local attraction and closing errors adjusted by Bowditch's method. Levelling uses a level and staff to find differences in height by rise and fall or height of instrument methods, giving reduced levels for contour and profile drawing. Precision requires careful setting up, back sights and foresights, checking arithmetic and recording in field books. Equipment includes chains, tapes, pegs, arrows, ranging poles and GPS.
sla_notes_illustrations: For a levelling exercise, the back sight is 1.45 m and the foresight 2.10 m, so the fall is 0.65 m and if the first reduced level is 100.00 m the next is 99.35 m.
sla_notes_daily_life: Surveying is used in planning roads, farms, plots and drainage in the community.
sla_exercise: What instrument measures bearings in traversing?::The prismatic compass.||If the back sight is 1.20 m and foresight is 0.80 m, what is the rise?::0.40 m.||Name the two levelling methods.::Height of instrument and rise and fall.

learning_activity_name: Acquire, present and interpret geographical data through charts, graphs, maps and diagrams (choropleth, scatter plots, dot maps, flow line etc.) for planning and decision making
sla_name: Geographical Data: Acquisition, Presentation and Interpretation
sla_assessment_criteria: Geographical data are well acquired, presented and interpreted for planning and decision making.
sla_teaching_aids: Online data|Notebook|Recording tools (tape recorder / camera / mobile phone)|Software for data analysis (NVIVO / SPSS / GIS)|Online resources on research skills
sla_references: TET(2023), GEOGRAPHY SYLLABUS FOR ADVANCED SECONDARY EDUCATION FORM V-VI, TET, DAR ES SALAAM
sla_notes_intro: Geographical data are facts collected to describe places and phenomena. They are acquired, presented and interpreted to support planning and decisions.
sla_notes_details: Data are acquired from primary sources (observation, questionnaires, interviews, measurements) and secondary sources (books, censuses, maps, online databases). Presentation techniques include bar and line graphs, pie charts, scatter graphs, choropleth maps (shading by density), dot maps, flow line maps, proportional symbols and diagrams. Interpretation involves describing patterns, trends and relationships, explaining causes and drawing conclusions with limitations. Software such as spreadsheets and GIS support analysis, and results guide decisions on land use, water supply and settlements.
sla_notes_illustrations: Population densities of regions are shaded on a choropleth map: darker shading for Dar es Salaam and lighter for Katavi, and the interpretation explains high density by economic activity and services.
sla_notes_daily_life: Local governments use such data to plan schools, water points and health centres.
sla_exercise: Name two primary sources of data.::Questionnaires and field observation.||What does a choropleth map show?::Variation of a quantity by area using shading or colour.||What is a flow line map used for?::Showing movement, such as trade or migration, by lines of different widths.

learning_activity_name: Identify a geographical challenge in society and design a project to address it
sla_name: Identifying a Geographical Challenge and Designing a Project
sla_assessment_criteria: The geographical challenge is identified and the project to address it is well designed.
sla_teaching_aids: Recording tools (tape recorder / notebook / camera / mobile phone)|Software for data analysis (NVIVO / SPSS / GIS)
sla_references: TET(2023), GEOGRAPHY SYLLABUS FOR ADVANCED SECONDARY EDUCATION FORM V-VI, TET, DAR ES SALAAM
sla_notes_intro: A geographical project studies a real problem in the community and proposes solutions. Form Five students identify the problem and design the project.
sla_notes_details: Steps are identifying a challenge (soil erosion, floods, water shortage, waste management), formulating a research problem, objectives and questions, reviewing literature, choosing methods (observation, questionnaires, interviews, mapping) and sampling, planning the schedule and budget and recording tools (camera, notebook, phone, GIS). A case study helps students see how challenges are addressed. The project proposal is presented and reviewed by the teacher.
sla_notes_illustrations: A group notices flooding near the school, states the objective as finding causes and effects of flooding in the ward, and designs a survey and mapping exercise.
sla_notes_daily_life: Research skills gained help students to contribute to community planning and problem solving.
sla_exercise: Name one example of a geographical challenge.::Soil erosion (or flooding, water shortage).||What are the first steps of designing a project?::Identify the problem and state the objectives.||Give two tools used for data recording.::Notebook and camera.

learning_activity_name: Describe rocks and the rock cycle (meaning, characteristics, types, formation, weathering and soil formation)
sla_assessment_criteria: Rocks and the rock cycle are well described.
sla_teaching_aids: Diagrams of the rocks|The rock cycle|Samples of different types of soil|Online resources on rocks|Maps|Models of rocks|ICT devices with contents on rocks
sla_references: TET(2023), GEOGRAPHY SYLLABUS FOR ADVANCED SECONDARY EDUCATION FORM V-VI, TET, DAR ES SALAAM
sla_notes_intro: Rocks are natural solid masses of minerals that form the earth's crust. The rock cycle shows how rocks change from one type to another over time.
sla_notes_details: Igneous rocks form from cooled magma or lava (granite, basalt), sedimentary rocks form from compacted and cemented sediments (sandstone, limestone) and metamorphic rocks form from heat and pressure on existing rocks (marble, slate, gneiss). The rock cycle links processes of weathering, erosion, deposition, compaction, metamorphism and melting. Weathering (physical, chemical and biological) breaks rocks and, with organic matter, forms soil with horizons A, B and C. Soil characteristics depend on parent rock, climate, relief, organisms and time and are important for agriculture.
sla_notes_illustrations: Granite exposed at the surface weathers, its sediments are carried to a lake, compacted into sandstone, heated deep underground into quartzite and eventually melted into magma to form new igneous rock.
sla_notes_daily_life: Farmers choose crops according to soil type, and builders use rocks such as limestone for cement and gravel for roads.
sla_exercise: Name the three main types of rocks.::Igneous, sedimentary and metamorphic.||Give an example of a metamorphic rock.::Marble (or slate).||What is weathering?::The breaking down of rocks in place by weather and organisms.

learning_activity_name: Explain the basic concepts of hydrology (meaning, types and importance)
sla_assessment_criteria: The basic concepts of hydrology are well explained.
sla_teaching_aids: Diagrams of the hydrological cycle|Water|Samples of different types of soil|Online resources on hydrology|The hydrological cycle|Topographical maps
sla_references: TET(2023), GEOGRAPHY SYLLABUS FOR ADVANCED SECONDARY EDUCATION FORM V-VI, TET, DAR ES SALAAM
sla_notes_intro: Hydrology is the scientific study of water on and below the earth's surface. It explains its occurrence, movement and use.
sla_notes_details: Types of hydrology include surface water hydrology (rivers, lakes), groundwater hydrology (aquifers, springs), hydrometeorology (rainfall and evaporation) and environmental and urban hydrology. Basic concepts include catchment area, river discharge, water table, runoff, infiltration and precipitation. Importance includes water supply for domestic, agricultural and industrial use, hydropower generation, flood control, planning and water resources management, and environmental protection.
sla_notes_illustrations: By measuring the discharge of the Pangani or Rufiji River, hydrologists decide how much water can be used for irrigation and hydropower without harming the ecosystem.
sla_notes_daily_life: Understanding hydrology helps communities to manage wells, boreholes and rainwater harvesting.
sla_exercise: Define hydrology.::The study of water on and below the earth's surface, its movement and distribution.||What is a water table?::The upper level of groundwater in rocks.||State one importance of hydrology.::It helps in planning water supply and flood control.

main_competence_name: Demonstrate mastery of the structure of the Earth
specific_competence_name: Demonstrate an understanding of the basics of hydrology and the hydrological cycle
learning_activity_name: Describe the hydrological cycle (Outputs, storages, flows and underground water)
sla_assessment_criteria: The hydrological cycle is well described.
sla_references: TET(2023), GEOGRAPHY SYLLABUS FOR ADVANCED SECONDARY EDUCATION FORM V-VI, TET, DAR ES SALAAM
sla_notes_intro: The hydrological cycle is the continuous movement of water between the oceans, atmosphere and land. It is driven by solar energy and gravity.
sla_notes_details: Inputs are precipitation and outputs are evaporation, transpiration (together evapotranspiration), runoff into rivers and seas and groundwater outflow. Storages include the oceans, ice caps, lakes, soil moisture, vegetation and groundwater aquifers. Flows include infiltration, percolation, throughflow, surface runoff and stream flow. Underground water is stored in aquifers and exits as springs and wells. Human activities such as damming, irrigation, deforestation, urbanisation and pollution affect the cycle.
sla_notes_illustrations: Water evaporates from Lake Victoria, condenses as clouds, falls as rain, infiltrates the soil, flows into the Kagera River and returns to the lake, completing one circuit.
sla_notes_daily_life: Farming calendars depend on the cycle because rains come at particular seasons.
sla_exercise: What drives the hydrological cycle?::Solar energy and gravity.||Name two water storages.::Oceans and groundwater (aquifers, lakes).||How does deforestation affect the cycle?::It reduces infiltration and transpiration and increases runoff.

main_competence_name: Demonstrate mastery of skills and techniques in Geography
learning_activity_name: Use the principles of map interpretation (visualizing symbols, signs, understanding themes, direction and association) to infer geographical features
sla_assessment_criteria: The principles of map interpretation are well used to infer geographical features.
sla_references: TET(2023), GEOGRAPHY SYLLABUS FOR ADVANCED SECONDARY EDUCATION FORM V-VI, TET, DAR ES SALAAM
sla_notes_intro: Map interpretation is reading a map to understand the geography of an area. It relies on a set of principles.
sla_notes_details: Principles include visualising symbols and signs using the key, understanding themes (relief, drainage, vegetation, settlement, transport, land use), determining direction using the north arrow and bearings, scale and distance, and association, which relates features to explain their occurrence (for example settlements near rivers or along roads). Contours show relief: closely spaced contours indicate a steep slope and widely spaced a gentle slope. Inference means deducing information such as economic activities, climate and history from patterns.
sla_notes_illustrations: On a topographical map, closely packed contours on the west, a river flowing eastward and scattered huts suggest a highland source of water and farming communities on the lower ground.
sla_notes_daily_life: Map skills are used when finding places, planning routes, choosing where to build or farm and using GPS navigation.
sla_exercise: What does a key or legend show?::The meaning of the symbols used on the map.||What do closely spaced contours indicate?::A steep slope.||What is association in map interpretation?::Relating features to explain their occurrence.

learning_activity_name: Apply the techniques of photograph interpretation to analyse geographical phenomena
sla_assessment_criteria: The techniques of photograph interpretation are well applied to analyse geographical phenomena.
sla_teaching_aids: Black-and-white|Coloured photographs|ICT devices with contents on photograph|GIS|GPS|ICT simulation tools on photograph
sla_references: TET(2023), GEOGRAPHY SYLLABUS FOR ADVANCED SECONDARY EDUCATION FORM V-VI, TET, DAR ES SALAAM
sla_notes_intro: Photographs of the earth's surface, taken from the ground or from the air, are used to study geographical phenomena. Interpretation is the analysis of what they show.
sla_notes_details: Types are ground (terrestrial) photographs, oblique aerial photographs and vertical aerial photographs, in black and white and colour. Techniques include identifying the type of photo, sketching the main features, dividing into foreground, middle ground and background, describing relief, drainage, vegetation, land use and settlement, and explaining relationships and possible human impacts. Clues are shape, size, tone, texture, pattern and shadow. Remote sensing and satellite images with GIS extend the method.
sla_notes_illustrations: An oblique photograph shows a river with meanders and wide flat land with rice fields in the foreground and hills in the background, so the interpreter concludes that the area is a flood plain used for farming.
sla_notes_daily_life: Photographs and satellite images are used in planning, disaster monitoring and mapping the growth of towns.
sla_exercise: Name two types of aerial photographs.::Vertical and oblique.||What are the three parts of a ground photograph to describe?::Foreground, middle ground and background.||State one clue used to identify features on a photograph.::Shape, tone, texture, pattern or shadow.

sla_notes_details: Students collect and analyse data, present it in tables, graphs and maps, interpret the findings, draw conclusions and give recommendations, and write the report with an abstract, introduction, objectives, methodology, findings, conclusion and references.
